claims.title: Mali's reach and the rise of Kaabu
claims.summary: The Mali Empire expanded west into the region, traditionally under Sundiata Keita's general Tiramakhan Traoré; the conquered lands became Kaabu (Gabu), a Mandinka province that would outlast Mali itself.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1235-mali-s-reach-and-the-rise-of-kaabu, claim TL:GNB:event:1235:mali-s-reach-and-the-rise-of-kaabu, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Kaabu becomes an independent federation
claims.summary: As Mali declined, Kaabu emerged as an independent federation of Mandinka kingdoms led by the Nyancho warrior nobility, centred on Kansala and dominant across the Senegambian interior.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1400-kaabu-becomes-an-independent-federation, claim TL:GNB:event:1400:kaabu-becomes-an-independent-federation, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The coastal and island peoples
claims.summary: The coast and rivers held the Balanta, Jola, Fula, Papel, Manjaco and Biafada, while the offshore Bijagós formed matrilineal warrior societies of seafarers and raiders — a fragmented mosaic of peoples and small states.

sources.label: A Guide to the History of Recognition: Guinea-Bissau
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian

claims.title: The Battle of Kansala ends Kaabu
claims.summary: A Fula army linked to Alfa Molo besieged and destroyed the Kaabu capital of Kansala; tradition holds the mansaba Dianke Walli blew up the gunpowder store rather than surrender, ending Kaabu and giving rise to the Fula kingdom of Fuladu.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1867-the-battle-of-kansala-ends-kaabu, claim TL:GNB:event:1867:the-battle-of-kansala-ends-kaabu, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Portuguese ships reach the Rivers of Guinea
claims.summary: Expeditions under Alvise Cadamosto, sailing for Portugal's Prince Henry the Navigator, explored the coast and estuaries of Guinea, opening European trade in the labyrinth of rivers that gave the region its name.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1455-portuguese-ships-reach-the-rivers-of-guinea, claim TL:GNB:event:1455:portuguese-ships-reach-the-rivers-of-guinea, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Cacheu fortified as a slaving station
claims.summary: The Portuguese established a fortified post at Cacheu, which became the principal slave-trading centre on the rivers; captives were funnelled through it to Cape Verde and across the Atlantic.

sources.label: A Guide to the History of Recognition: Guinea-Bissau

claims.title: The Atlantic slave trade via Cape Verde
claims.summary: Administered through Cape Verde, the Rivers of Guinea became a major source of enslaved people; tens of thousands were carried to the islands' plantations and onward to the Americas, especially during the Iberian Union (1580–1640).

claims.title: Bissau founded as a fortified post
claims.summary: The Portuguese founded Bissau in 1765 as a military and slave-trading station; it grew into the region's main commercial centre and, in 1942, replaced Bolama as the colonial capital.

sources.label: A Guide to the History of Recognition: Guinea-Bissau
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian

claims.title: Slavery abolished, contract labour follows
claims.summary: Portugal abolished slavery in its territories, but replaced it with coercive "contract labour" arrangements; the transatlantic trade through Guinea's rivers had already declined across the nineteenth century.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1869-slavery-abolished-contract-labour-follows, claim TL:GNB:event:1869:slavery-abolished-contract-labour-follows, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Guinea separated from Cape Verde
claims.summary: Portuguese Guinea was detached from Cape Verde and constituted as a separate colony; after the Berlin Conference its frontiers with French possessions were fixed by agreement with France.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1879-guinea-separated-from-cape-verde, claim TL:GNB:event:1879:guinea-separated-from-cape-verde, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: A separate military district
claims.summary: Lisbon made Guinea a distinct military district to promote "effective occupation", but Portuguese authority still reached little beyond the coastal forts and trading towns.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1892-a-separate-military-district, claim TL:GNB:event:1892:a-separate-military-district, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Teixeira Pinto's pacification of the mainland
claims.summary: The officer João Teixeira Pinto, with the auxiliary Abdul Injai, led brutal campaigns that crushed mainland resistance and brought the interior under Portuguese control for the first time.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1912-teixeira-pinto-s-pacification-of-the-mainland, claim TL:GNB:event:1912:teixeira-pinto-s-pacification-of-the-mainland, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The Bijagós islands subdued
claims.summary: After repeated campaigns against the seafaring Bijagós, the Estado Novo finally imposed control over the archipelago in 1935–1936, completing the conquest more than four centuries after first Portuguese contact.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1936-the-bijagos-islands-subdued, claim TL:GNB:event:1936:the-bijagos-islands-subdued, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Renamed an "overseas province"
claims.summary: Responding to international criticism, Portugal reclassified Guinea and its other colonies as "overseas provinces", recasting empire as an integral part of Portugal while colonial conditions persisted.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1951-renamed-an-overseas-province, claim TL:GNB:event:1951:renamed-an-overseas-province, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Amílcar Cabral founds the PAIGC
claims.summary: The agronomist Amílcar Cabral and a small group founded the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), the movement that would lead the struggle against Portuguese rule.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1956-amilcar-cabral-founds-the-paigc, claim TL:GNB:event:1956:amilcar-cabral-founds-the-paigc, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The Pidjiguiti massacre
claims.summary: Portuguese police opened fire on striking dockworkers at the Pidjiguiti quay in Bissau, killing scores; the killings turned the PAIGC away from peaceful protest and toward armed struggle.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1959-the-pidjiguiti-massacre, claim TL:GNB:event:1959:the-pidjiguiti-massacre, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The war of independence begins
claims.summary: The PAIGC launched its armed campaign with attacks on Portuguese garrisons in the south, opening a guerrilla war that would steadily expand the "liberated zones" across the interior.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1963-the-war-of-independence-begins, claim TL:GNB:event:1963:the-war-of-independence-begins, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Cabral assassinated in Conakry
claims.summary: Amílcar Cabral was shot dead at a roadblock in Conakry by a disgruntled PAIGC member, Inocêncio Kani, and others, in a plot widely linked to Portuguese agents — eight months before independence was proclaimed.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1973-cabral-assassinated-in-conakry, claim TL:GNB:event:1973:cabral-assassinated-in-conakry, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Independence declared at Boé
claims.summary: The PAIGC's People's National Assembly unilaterally proclaimed the Republic of Guinea-Bissau in the liberated southeast; the new state was rapidly recognised abroad and endorsed by a 93–7 UN General Assembly vote in November.

claims.title: Portugal recognises independence
claims.summary: Following the Carnation Revolution and an accord at Algiers, Portugal formally recognised Guinea-Bissau's independence on 10 September 1974; the United States acknowledged it the same day, with Luís Cabral as first president.

sources.label: A Guide to the History of Recognition: Guinea-Bissau

claims.title: Nino Vieira seizes power
claims.summary: A coup led by João Bernardo "Nino" Vieira overthrew President Luís Cabral, fracturing the planned union with Cape Verde and beginning Vieira's dominance of national politics.

sources.label: A Guide to the History of Recognition: Guinea-Bissau
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian

claims.title: First multi-party elections
claims.summary: After the introduction of multi-party politics in 1991, Guinea-Bissau held its first competitive elections in 1994, which confirmed Vieira as president — though military factionalism persisted.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1994-first-multi-party-elections, claim TL:GNB:event:1994:first-multi-party-elections, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: The civil war
claims.summary: A military mutiny led by Ansumane Mané escalated into a civil war that drew in Senegalese and Guinean troops, devastated Bissau and displaced hundreds of thousands before Vieira was ousted in May 1999.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-1998-the-civil-war, claim TL:GNB:event:1998:the-civil-war, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Vieira assassinated
claims.summary: Having returned to the presidency in 2005, João Bernardo Vieira was assassinated by soldiers in March 2009, hours after the killing of the army chief of staff — a vivid sign of the army's grip on politics.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Guinea-Bissau: From the Mandinka empire of Kaabu and the coastal peoples of the Rivers of Guinea, through Portuguese slaving forts, a very late colonial conquest, and Amílcar Cabral's guerrilla war, to independence in 1973–1974 and decades of coups.", terralore.co/country/GNB/chronicle#ev-2009-vieira-assassinated, claim TL:GNB:event:2009:vieira-assassinated, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Coup amid the cocaine trade
claims.summary: A military coup interrupted a presidential election in April 2012, deepening a pattern of intervention by a politicised army increasingly entangled with cocaine trafficking.

claims.title: A cocaine transit "narco-state"
claims.summary: Weak institutions, porous borders and an archipelago of uninhabited islands made Guinea-Bissau a major transit point for Latin American cocaine bound for Europe; the UN described it as the first African "narco-state", with the drug trade rivalling the legal economy.
